idiom_name: export inner.member in a class extending the service trait
implementation_notes: Scala 3's export clause forwards named members of an inner service in one line (export inner.health), while members needing control are ordinary overrides, so the forwarded surface is generated by the compiler and stays in sync with the declaration; callers see the same trait and nothing else changes. This replaces the Scala 2 idiom of stacking traits, and for RPC services the framework-level equivalent is a gRPC interceptor; the JDK dynamic proxy remains available when the interface is Java.
code_sketch:
trait ServiceApi:
  def call(request: Request): Response
  def health(): Boolean

final class ServiceProxy(inner: ServiceApi, metrics: Metrics) extends ServiceApi:
  export inner.health                       // forwarded by the compiler

  def call(request: Request): Response =    // control only where needed
    val started = System.nanoTime()
    try inner.call(request)                 // same contract
    finally metrics.record("call", System.nanoTime() - started)
pitfalls: Exporting a member and overriding the same name is a compile error: export only the members you do not intercept, and keep the export list next to the overrides.
An export binds to the given instance at construction, so a service that can be replaced needs an indirection (a def or a var behind the proxy).
Exported members are inherited without a further override, so a subclass cannot selectively re-intercept what the export already fixed.

variants.name: Stackable trait modifiers (abstract override) as the interception chain
variants.idiom_name: trait X extends ServiceApi { abstract override def call = ... super.call ... } mixed in at construction
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala 2 idiom builds the proxy chain from traits: each policy trait extends the service trait, declares the intercepted member abstract override and calls super around its own behaviour, so mixing traits in a chosen order assembles a different chain over the same service - the stackable modifications form of the pattern and still the standard way to compose cross-cutting behaviour in Scala 2 codebases. Linearization decides the order, so the mixin composition at the construction site is the configuration.
pitfalls: Only members declared abstract override can intercept, and each policy trait must be mixed in exactly once; stacking the same trait twice double-counts or fails to compile.
Linearization order decides which policy runs first and which sees the final result - document the canonical mixin order or the chain silently changes meaning.
The chain is fixed at construction: unlike a control-plane-driven proxy, a stack assembled this way cannot be reconfigured at runtime.
